questions.q: In a genetic algorithm, what is the job of the fitness function?
choices: Score a candidate so better ones can be favored
Choose which two candidates become parents
Randomly flip bits to add new genetic material
Decide how many generations the run will last
questions.explain: The fitness function scores each candidate (higher is better). Selection then uses those scores to favor fitter candidates. In this program, fitness() counts the 1s.

questions.q: In geneticBinary.cpp, what plays the role of a single gene?
choices: One '0' or '1' character in a string
One 20-character string
The vector of 50 strings
One pass of the generation loop
questions.explain: A gene is one position in the chromosome, here one char bit. The 20-character string is the chromosome, the vector is the population, and one loop pass is a generation.

questions.q: In geneticBinary.cpp, what does one generation correspond to?
choices: One iteration of the for (generation ...) loop
One call to crossover()
One tournament inside selectParent()
One bit flip inside mutate()
questions.explain: Each pass of the generation loop evaluates the population, keeps the elite, breeds 49 children and replaces the population.

questions.q: The GA in geneticBinary.cpp is guaranteed to reach fitness 20/20 before it stops.
questions.explain: A GA is a random heuristic. This one stops after 100 generations no matter what, so it can end without finding 20/20, and two runs can give different results.

questions.q: The fitness function is the only part of the program that knows which problem is being solved; selection, crossover and mutation would work unchanged on a different bit-string problem.
questions.explain: Selection only compares fitness scores, and crossover and mutation only move or flip bits. Swapping in a different fitness() changes the problem.

questions.q: How many different 20-bit strings are there (the size of this program's search space)?
With 50 individuals per generation and at most 100 generations, about how many strings does one run evaluate at most?
questions.explain: About 100 x 50 = 5,000, a tiny fraction of the 1,048,576 possible strings. That is the point of using a GA instead of brute force.

questions.q: A person can solve 'maximize the number of 1s' instantly. Why is it still a useful demo problem for a GA?
choices: You can see progress directly as fitness out of 20
No other method is able to solve it
It has exactly one candidate solution
Its fitness function needs no computation at all
questions.explain: You always know how close the GA is (fitness out of 20), so you can watch selection, crossover and mutation work. The same code could solve a harder problem with a different fitness().

questions.q: What does fitness() return for the chromosome 11010011100000111101?
questions.explain: Fitness is the number of '1' characters: 1101 has 3, 0011 has 2, 1000 has 1, 0011 has 2, 1101 has 3. Total 11.

questions.q: What is the expected fitness of one string made by randomChromosome()?
questions.explain: Each of the 20 bits is '1' with probability 1/2, so the fitness is Binomial(20, 0.5) with mean 20 x 0.5 = 10.

questions.q: What is the standard deviation of the fitness of one random 20-bit string (each bit '1' with probability 1/2)? Give two decimal places.
questions.explain: sd = sqrt(20 x 0.5 x 0.5) = sqrt(5), about 2.24.

questions.q: In the random first generation of 50 strings, what is the best fitness usually around?
choices: 6 to 8
questions.explain: 10 is the average of one string. The best of 50 is higher: there is about a 95% chance that at least one scores 14 or more, and about a 26% chance that one scores 16 or more.

questions.q: In randomChromosome(), each bit is '1' with probability 1/2, independently of the other bits.
questions.explain: Each bit comes from its own randomInt(0, 1) call: 0 gives '0' and 1 gives '1'.

questions.q: About how likely is it that the optimum (all 1s) is already in the random generation 0 of 50 strings?
choices: About 50/2^20, roughly 0.005%
About 1/20, roughly 5%
About 1/50, roughly 2%
About 1/2, roughly 50%
questions.explain: Each string is all 1s with probability 2^-20. Then 1 - (1 - 2^-20)^50 is about 50/2^20, about 4.8 x 10^-5.

questions.q: fitness() takes time proportional to STRING_LENGTH, because it looks at every character once.
questions.explain: It is a range-based for over the characters, so it runs in O(L) time.

questions.q: How does selectParent() choose a parent?
choices: The best of 3 randomly picked individuals
The best individual in the whole population
One individual picked uniformly at random
One of the top 3 individuals, at random
questions.explain: It is tournament selection of size 3: one random pick, then 2 more in the loop, and the fittest of those 3 is returned.

questions.q: Within a single tournament in selectParent(), the same individual can be picked more than once.
questions.explain: Each pick is an independent randomInt(0, POPULATION_SIZE - 1), so picks are with replacement.

questions.q: A tournament picks, in this order, X (fitness 13), Y (fitness 16), Z (fitness 16). Which individual does selectParent() return?
choices: Y
Z
X
Y or Z, chosen at random
questions.explain: Start with X (13). Y: 16 > 13, so Y. Z: 16 > 16 is false, so Y stays. The strict > means ties keep the earlier pick.

questions.q: Population size 50, tournament size 3, no ties. To 4 decimal places, what is the probability that the unique best individual wins one tournament?
questions.explain: The best wins whenever it is picked at least once: 1 - (49/50)^3 is about 0.0588. A uniform random pick would give only 0.02.

questions.q: How many tournaments does selectParent() run in one generation of this program?
questions.explain: There are 49 children (50 minus the 1 elite), and each needs 2 tournaments (parent1 and parent2): 49 x 2 = 98.

questions.q: Assume no ties. When can the unique worst individual win a tournament?
choices: All 3 picks are that individual
It is the first of the 3 picks
The other two picks tie each other
It can never win a tournament
questions.explain: Any other pick would beat it. So it wins only when all 3 picks are the worst individual, with probability (1/50)^3 = 0.000008.

questions.q: What happens if you increase the tournament size?
choices: More selection pressure
Faster loss of diversity
Parents are chosen purely at random
The best fitness can start to decrease
questions.explain: Bigger tournaments return the population's best more often, so improvement is faster at first but diversity collapses faster. Random parents would come from a size-1 tournament. Elitism still keeps the best fitness from dropping.

questions.q: With a tournament size of 1, parents would be chosen purely at random and there would be no selection pressure.
questions.explain: One pick means there is nothing to compare, so fitness plays no part in choosing parents and fitness just drifts.

questions.q: The two tournaments for one child can both return the same individual. Then the child is a copy of that parent, apart from any mutation.
questions.explain: The two tournaments are independent. Crossing a string with itself gives the same string back, at any cut point.

questions.q: parent1 = 10101010101010101010, parent2 = 11111111110000000000, point = 5. What child string does crossover() return?
questions.explain: parent1.substr(0, 5) = 10101 and parent2.substr(5) = 111110000000000 (indices 5 to 19). Joined, that gives 10101111110000000000.

questions.q: parent1 is all 0s (00000000000000000000), parent2 is all 1s (11111111111111111111), and the cut point is 7. What is the child's fitness before mutation?
questions.explain: The first 7 characters come from parent1 (all 0s) and the last 13 come from parent2 (all 1s), so fitness = 13.

questions.q: With STRING_LENGTH = 20, how many different cut points can crossover() choose?
questions.explain: point = randomInt(1, STRING_LENGTH - 1) = randomInt(1, 19), inclusive: 19 values.

questions.q: If crossover() were allowed to pick point = 0, what would the child be?
choices: An exact copy of parent2
An exact copy of parent1
An empty string
The complement of parent1
questions.explain: parent1.substr(0, 0) is empty, and parent2.substr(0) is all of parent2. The range [1, 19] makes sure each parent gives at least one gene.

questions.q: If every individual in the population has '0' at index 7, crossover can still produce a child with '1' at index 7.
questions.explain: Crossover only rearranges bit values the parents already have. Only mutation can create a bit value the whole population lacks.

questions.q: Each call to crossover() in this program produces two children: head-of-parent1 + tail-of-parent2, and the mirror image.
questions.explain: It returns only parent1.substr(0, point) + parent2.substr(point). The mirror child is never built.

questions.q: In this program, how often is crossover used when making a child?
choices: Always; every child comes from crossover
With probability 0.01 for each child
Only when the two parents are different
With probability 0.5 for each child
questions.explain: There is no crossover-rate parameter. Every child is crossover(parent1, parent2), then mutated.

questions.q: A new random cut point is chosen for each child.
questions.explain: randomInt(1, STRING_LENGTH - 1) is called inside crossover(), which runs once per child.

questions.q: What does MUTATION_RATE = 0.01 mean in this program?
choices: Each bit independently flips with probability 0.01
Each child is mutated with probability 0.01
Exactly one bit flips in 1% of all children
1% of the population is replaced by random strings
questions.explain: mutate() loops over every bit and flips it when randomDouble() < MUTATION_RATE. The rate is per bit, not per chromosome.

questions.q: With 20 bits and MUTATION_RATE = 0.01, what is the expected number of bits mutation flips in one child?
With 20 bits and MUTATION_RATE = 0.01, what is the probability that a child has no bits flipped at all? Give 3 decimal places.
questions.explain: 0.99^20 is about 0.818. So about 82% of children are not mutated, and only about 18% get at least one flip (not 1%).

questions.q: About how many bit flips does mutation cause across one whole generation (all the children together)?
questions.explain: 49 children x 0.2 expected flips each = 9.8. The elite is never mutated.

questions.q: Mutation can lower a child's fitness.
questions.explain: Mutation is random. Flipping a 0 to 1 helps, and flipping a 1 to 0 hurts. Selection is what keeps the good changes.

questions.q: If MUTATION_RATE were raised to 0.05 (STRING_LENGTH still 20), what would be the expected number of bit flips per child?
What is the main purpose of mutation in this GA?
choices: Add new bit values and keep diversity
Choose the fittest parents more often
Keep the best fitness from ever dropping
Combine the parts of two parents
questions.explain: Mutation adds new genetic material so the population can escape states where crossover alone is stuck. Selection favors fit parents, elitism prevents drops, and crossover combines parents.

questions.q: Late in a run, every individual is the same 19/20 string, with a single 0 at position j. To 4 decimal places, what is the probability that one child comes out as 20/20?
questions.explain: Crossover of identical parents changes nothing, so mutation must flip bit j and none of the other 19: 0.01 x 0.99^19 is about 0.0083. With 49 children that is about a 1/3 chance per generation.

questions.q: The elite individual copied into newPopulation is mutated just like the children.
questions.explain: best is pushed into newPopulation directly, and only child is passed to mutate(), so the elite is copied unchanged.

questions.q: What is a consequence of elitism in this program?
choices: The best fitness never decreases between generations
Every child is at least as fit as its parents
The population can never lose its diversity
The optimum is always found within 100 generations
questions.explain: Each generation's best is copied unchanged into the next one, so the printed best fitness is non-decreasing. Children can still be worse than their parents.

questions.q: How many children are created by crossover and mutation in each generation?
questions.explain: newPopulation starts with the 1 elite, and children are added while its size is below 50: 50 - 1 = 49.

questions.q: Which of these can end the program's run?
choices: Some individual reaches fitness 20
All 100 generations finish
The best fitness stays the same for 10 generations
All individuals become identical
questions.explain: The loop breaks when fitness(best) == STRING_LENGTH, or ends after generations 0 to 99. The program never checks for stagnation or convergence.

questions.q: If all 100 generations finish without a 20/20 string, the program prints a message saying the optimum was not found.
questions.explain: Only success prints a message ("Optimal solution found!"). When the budget runs out, the loop just ends silently.

questions.q: Within one generation, in what order does main() do these steps?
choices: Find best, elitism, select, crossover, mutate, replace
Select, crossover, mutate, find best, elitism, replace
Elitism, find best, select, mutate, crossover, replace
Find best, select, crossover, elitism, mutate, replace
questions.explain: STEP 3 finds and prints the best (and stops if it is 20). STEP 4 pushes it into newPopulation. STEP 5 repeats select x2, crossover, mutate, add. Then population = newPopulation.

questions.q: What does the line printed for 'Generation 0' describe?
choices: The random initial population
The first population made by crossover
The population after one round of mutation
Only the elite individual
questions.explain: Generation 0 is evaluated before any breeding, so its best comes from the 50 random strings made in STEP 1.

questions.q: When several individuals tie for the highest fitness, the STEP 3 scan keeps the one that appears first in the population.
questions.explain: best starts as population[0] and is replaced only when fitness(chromosome) > fitness(best). A tie does not replace it.

questions.q: Without elitism, the best fitness could go down from one generation to the next.
questions.explain: The best individual might win no tournament, or its children might be worse or damaged by mutation, so it could disappear.

questions.q: MUTATION_RATE is set to 0, and by bad luck every string in the initial population has '0' at index 7. What is the highest fitness the GA can ever reach?
questions.explain: Crossover only copies existing bit values, so index 7 stays '0' in every individual forever. Only mutation could change it.

questions.q: What happens if MUTATION_RATE is set to 1.0?
choices: Each child is the complement of its crossover result
Each child is basically an unrelated random string
Each child is an exact copy of its first parent
Exactly one bit flips in every single child
questions.explain: randomDouble() < 1.0 is always true, so every bit flips. Fit parents give unfit children. The elite still survives, so the best fitness does not drop.

questions.q: With MUTATION_RATE = 0.5, each child is essentially a random string, so the GA behaves like random search.
questions.explain: Each bit becomes a coin flip, which erases whatever selection and crossover produced.

questions.q: Which parts of this program mainly drive exploitation (focusing on what already works)?
choices: Tournament selection
Elitism
Mutation
Random initialization
questions.explain: Selection favors fitter parents, and elitism keeps the best. Mutation (and partly crossover) drives exploration.

questions.q: Too much exploitation (too little exploration) tends to cause what?
choices: Premature convergence
Random search
Undefined behavior
A std::out_of_range exception
questions.explain: Everyone becomes a copy of one decent but non-optimal string and nothing changes. Too much exploration gives random search instead.

questions.q: Raising MAX_GENERATIONS lets the GA reach 20/20 even when MUTATION_RATE is 0 and some bit position is '0' in every individual.
questions.explain: With no mutation, the missing '1' can never appear, so extra generations do not help.

questions.q: What is the main trade-off of a bigger POPULATION_SIZE?
choices: More diversity, but more work per generation
Less work per generation, but faster diversity loss
No effect, because only the best is ever kept
The best fitness becomes able to decrease
questions.explain: A bigger population keeps more diversity and usually needs fewer generations, but each generation costs more. A smaller one is cheaper but gets stuck more easily.

questions.q: What goes wrong if STRING_LENGTH is set to 1?
choices: crossover() calls randomInt(1, 0), so min > max
fitness() always returns 0 for every string
mutate() is no longer able to flip any bits
The population size also drops to 1
questions.explain: randomInt(1, STRING_LENGTH - 1) becomes randomInt(1, 0), and a uniform_int_distribution with min > max is undefined behavior. STRING_LENGTH must be at least 2.

questions.q: Keeping too many elites per generation leaves fewer new children and less exploration.
questions.explain: More elites keep more good solutions safe, but every elite slot is one less child, so there is less exploration.

questions.q: mt19937 is the standard C++ name for which pseudo-random number generator?
questions.explain: mt19937 is the 32-bit Mersenne Twister from <random>.

questions.q: What can randomInt(0, 1) return?
choices: 0 or 1
Always 0
A double in [0, 1)
questions.explain: uniform_int_distribution<int>(min, max) includes both endpoints.

questions.q: What range of values can randomDouble() return?
questions.explain: uniform_real_distribution<double>(0.0, 1.0) includes 0 and excludes 1.

questions.q: Because rng is seeded with random_device{}(), two runs of the program usually give different output.
questions.explain: random_device{}() gets a seed from the OS, so the generator starts in a different state on each run.

questions.q: How could you make every run of the program produce the same output, for example to debug it?
choices: Seed it with a constant, e.g. mt19937 rng(42);
Call random_device{}() twice instead of once
Create a new mt19937 inside every function
Use uniform_real_distribution everywhere
questions.explain: A fixed seed makes the generator produce the same sequence every run.

questions.q: If mutate() looped with for (char bit : chromosome) instead of for (char& bit : chromosome), what would happen?
choices: Mutation silently has no effect
The code no longer compiles
Every bit is flipped every time
The elite also gets mutated
questions.explain: Without the reference, bit is a copy, so flipping it does not change the string. The child comes back unmutated.

questions.q: In crossover(), what does parent2.substr(point) return?
choices: Everything from index point to the end
The first point characters
Only the character at index point
Characters 0 through point, inclusive
questions.explain: substr(pos) takes everything from pos to the end. substr(0, point) takes the first point characters (indices 0 to point - 1).

questions.q: For a 20-character string s, s.substr(20) throws std::out_of_range.
questions.explain: A position equal to the length is legal and returns "". Only a position greater than size(), such as s.substr(21), throws std::out_of_range.

questions.q: Why does selectParent() take its population as const vector<string>&?
choices: It avoids copying all 50 strings on each call
It lets the function reorder the population
It makes the 3 picks happen without replacement
It lets the function edit the chosen strings
questions.explain: The reference avoids a copy on each of the 98 calls per generation, and const blocks any changes. It has nothing to do with how picks are made.

questions.q: fitness() is recomputed every time two individuals are compared; for an expensive fitness function you would cache each individual's score.
questions.explain: Each comparison recomputes both sides, and the best's fitness is computed again when printing and checking. That is fine for an O(L) bit count but wasteful for a costly fitness function.
